newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl and German union leader agree coal compromise.
newsitem.headline: Kohl and German union leader agree coal compromise.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl and mining union leader Hans Berger reached a compromise on Thursday to avoid mass layoffs while sharply cutting back subsidies to the coal industry, Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said.
Berger hailed the deal as a success that met the union's main goals, and many of the protesting miners awaiting the news in nearby Cologne appeared ready to accept it.

The miners had virtually besieged Bonn's government quarter for three days this week, but withdrew on Wednesday after Kohl postponed talks planned for Tuesday at short notice, saying he would not negotiate in a climate of intimidation.
"The fight was worth it," Berger said, adding that he had the impression from union officials that the miners would accept the deal.

Speaking for the government, Bohl told reporters: "We have ensured the survival of the mining industry in a way that is economically acceptable...We have ensured changes in the mining industry can be carried out in a way that avoids mass layoffs."

The 8,000 or so pit workers from Saar state on the French border who spent the night in a tented village in the grounds of Cologne football stadium cheered when they heard the news and appeared to be getting ready to head home in a fleet of buses.
But it was not immediately clear how the biggest mining area in the Ruhr valley, whose miners briefly became violent in Bonn on Tuesday, would react.

Under the deal, the federal government agreed to provide more aid for the coal industry than planned for the next few years, but stuck to its original goal to slash subsidies from nine billion marks now to 3.8 billion ($2.2 billion) by 2005.
The pledge to avoid mass layoffs means the layoffs, totalling about 26,000 by the year 2000 and 46,000 by 2005, will be flanked by retraining or other measures to cushion the blow.

Miners in Germany's 18 pits walked out last Friday after Bonn announced the cuts, arguing that it could no longer afford to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is more than three times the world market price.
IG Bergbau had said the original plan would force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.

In a separate protest, thousands of builders were again massing on Berlin's Potsdamer Platz square, Europe's largest construction site, to protest against conditions which they say have put almost a quarter of Germany's 1.7 million builders out of work.
In Bonn, commuter traffic was flowing normally on Thursday for the first time since last week.

Police maintained a strong presence and kept crowd barriers at the ready. But only a handful of miners were left as a reminder of the thousands who unnerved the city earlier in the week with protests which briefly spilled over into violence.
The mountains of bottles, drinks cans, disposable plates and cigarette butts they left behind had largely been cleared away.

Some commentators cautioned Kohl against backing down too far and laying his government open to pressure from all sides to give up the strict budget discipline necessary to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The danger of an increasingly aggressive wave of demonstrations is completely real," the daily newspaper Die Welt said in Thursday's edition.
